seo.meta_title: Is '김 씨' the Same as 'Mr. Kim'? | Addressing Your Korean Boss
seo.meta_description: AI translates 'Mr. Kim' as '김 씨', but calling a manager that in Korea sounds disrespectful. Learn how Koreans address superiors with job titles.

ai_failure.situation: Writing an email or speaking to your team leader, Kim Minjun
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Turns 'Mr. Kim' into '김 씨' or '김민준 씨', treating 씨 as a polite equivalent of Mr./Ms.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: 씨 is polite only between equals or toward juniors. Surname + 씨 alone can even sound like you're addressing a laborer or a stranger you look down on. Superiors are called by their job title.

natural_solution.rule: Address superiors by job title + 님 (with or without the surname). Use full name + 씨 only for peers or juniors.

alternatives.phrase: 김 팀장님, 회의 자료 보내 드렸습니다.
alternatives.romanization: gim tim-jang-nim, hoe-ui ja-ryo bo-nae deu-ryeot-seum-ni-da
alternatives.context: Surname + title + 님 — the safe default for a superior
Title + 님 alone, the most common form in person

alternatives.phrase: 민준 씨, 이것 좀 확인해 줄래요?
alternatives.romanization: min-jun ssi, i-geot jom hwa-gin-hae jul-lae-yo
alternatives.context: Given name + 씨 — fine for a colleague at your level or below

nuance: In Korean workplaces, a person's position effectively becomes their name: 과장님, 팀장님, 대표님. Adding the surname (김 과장님) helps when there are several people with the same title. 씨 sits much lower than English 'Mr.' suggests — it is respectful between equals, but used upward it erases the hierarchy the listener expects to be acknowledged. And surname + 씨 alone (김 씨) is the riskiest form of all, often heard in condescending or impersonal contexts.
